item.title: InSAR from Scratch (VII): Implicit Phase Unwrapping via the Minimum Gradient Assumption
item.description:
The previous post built the machinery for how the unobserved state, position and instantaneous velocity, evolves between epochs, but sidestepped how it actually connects to the observed data: a wrapped, modulo-$2\pi$ phase. This post closes that gap, and in doing so runs into unwrapping again, this time solved in a completely different way than either of the previous two treatments in this series.

Three ways to handle the same problem, so far

It’s worth naming all three side by side, since this series keeps returning to the same underlying issue.

item.title: InSAR from Scratch (VI): The Instantaneous State and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Velocity Model
item.description: The previous post showed how to fold a new observation into an estimate without reprocessing the whole history, as long as the underlying parameter $x$ stays exactly time-invariant. That’s still the limiting assumption. This post lifts it: instead of a fixed velocity, we let the instantaneous velocity itself be a random process that is allowed to wander, smoothly, over time. Wang et al. (2026) call the resulting state vector, position plus instantaneous velocity, the instantaneous state (IS).

item.title: InSAR from Scratch (V): From Batch to Sequential Estimation
item.description: This post opens a second arc within the Probabilistic InSAR series. The previous post closed the first arc, built around Chang & Hanssen (2016): a null model, a library of alternatives, and a way to pick the best-supported one via hypothesis testing. That whole pipeline assumes a batch of data: you already have all $m$ epochs, and you fit one, time-invariant set of parameters to explain the entire period at once. This post starts asking what changes when new SAR acquisitions keep arriving and you want an answer now, not after reprocessing everything from scratch. This arc follows Wang, Brouwer, van Leijen & Hanssen (2026).

item.title: InSAR from Scratch (IV): Making Hundreds of Tests Cheap, and What to Test For
item.description:
This is the fourth post in the Probabilistic InSAR series. The previous post set up the testing machinery for comparing a null deformation model against a whole library of alternatives. Here we work out how to make that testing procedure cheap enough to run on millions of points, and what a realistic library of alternative models actually contains.

The cost problem

The testing procedure from the previous post sounds reasonable for one point and a handful of candidate models. item.title: InSAR from Scratch (II): The Functional-Stochastic Model
item.description:
This is the second post in the Probabilistic InSAR series. The previous post worked out what the interferometric phase actually contains, how it wraps, and how a stack of interferograms becomes a phase time series per pixel. Here we take that time series and turn it into an honest statistical estimation problem.

From a phase time series to a regression problem

Take a single point in space, one persistent scatterer, and look at its phase time series across $m$ SAR acquisitions, already converted to a deformation-equivalent quantity (millimeters, say) and referenced to a master acquisition and a reference point. Call this vector of observations $y \in \mathbb{R}^m$.

item.title: Regression under multicollinearity: PCR, PLS, and penalised methods
item.description: Ordinary least squares breaks down when $p \gg n$: the matrix $X^\top X$ becomes singular and $\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top Y$ does not exist. This post surveys four strategies for dealing with that problem. The first two (PCR and PLS) compress the predictors into a small number of components before regressing. The last two (Ridge and Lasso) keep all $p$ predictors but penalise large coefficients. They attack the same problem from opposite directions, and which one works best depends entirely on the structure of the signal in your data.

item.title: PCA is equivalent to a Linear Autoencoder
item.description:
Our objective is to compact the representation of data while minimizing the information loss using linear transformations.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

Given $n$ data vector $\{x_1, \dots, x_n\} \in \mathbb{R}^m$, assuming that are mean centered, and given a target number of dimensions $k < m$. PCA finds an orthonormal basis $\{u_1, \dots, u_k\} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ that explains most of the variation of the projected data. Let $U \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times k}$ the matrix whose columns are $u_j \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ is a matrix whose columns are the data vector $x_j \in \mathbb{R}^m$.
